comparisons.peer_topic: USPB Expense and Credit Loss Trends
comparisons.peer_summary: USPB expenses decreased 1% to $10 billion due to productivity savings and lower technology costs, while cost of credit increased to $8.6 billion (from $6.7 billion) primarily due to a 45% rise in net credit losses from maturing card vintages and macroeconomic pressures on lower FICO band customers, partially offset by a lower ACL build.
comparisons.comparison: Both BAC and C report that net credit losses were a primary driver of negative margin or cost of credit performance in Consumer Banking/USPB segments. BAC attributes its risk-adjusted margin decrease to higher net credit losses, while C reports a 45% rise in net credit losses driving an increase in cost of credit. However, C explicitly links this deterioration to the maturation of loan vintages and macroeconomic pressures on lower FICO customers, whereas BAC cites higher net credit losses as the primary driver of the 85 bps margin decline without specifying vintage maturity or FICO band details in the selected text.

sentences.text: Total risk-adjusted margin decreased 85 bps primarily driven by higher net credit losses, partially offset by higher net interest margin and higher net fee income.
Cost of credit increased to $8.6 billion, compared to $6.7 billion in the prior year.

The increase was driven by higher net credit losses (up 45%), primarily reflecting the continued maturation of multiple cards loan vintages originated in recent years, as well as macroeconomic pressures related to the elevated inflationary and interest rate environment impacting both cards portfolios, with lower FICO band customers primarily driving the increase.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion in 2024 from $1.14 billion in 2023, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures discuss credit losses in their respective credit card portfolios as a key financial metric. BAC reports that higher net credit losses drove a decrease in consumer lending risk-adjusted margin. GS reports that provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio. While both identify net charge-offs/losses in credit cards as a significant cost headwind, BAC frames it as a margin compression factor within consumer banking, whereas GS frames it as a provision expense increase within Platform Solutions.

sentences.text: Total risk-adjusted margin decreased 85 bps primarily driven by higher net credit losses, partially offset by higher net interest margin and higher net fee income.
Provision for credit losses was $1.54 billion for 2024, compared with $1.14 billion for 2023.
Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).

comparisons.peer_summary: Card income increased, reflecting higher net interchange on increased debit and credit card sales volume, as well as higher annual fees in CCB, partially offset by an increase in amortization related to new account origination costs.
comparisons.comparison: BAC and JPM both highlight that increased card purchase volumes were a key positive driver for their respective card businesses, although the financial outcomes differed. BAC reports increased debit and credit card purchase volumes reflecting higher consumer spending, which occurred alongside a decrease in risk-adjusted margin due to credit losses. JPM similarly reports increased debit and credit card sales volume driving higher card income (net interchange), partially offset by costs. Both companies identify volume growth as a central business driver, but BAC's volume growth did not prevent margin decline due to credit losses, whereas JPM's volume growth contributed to income growth.

sentences.text: Total credit card purchase volumes increased $5.7 billion to $368.9 billion, and debit card purchase volumes increased $29.9 billion to $557.0 billion, reflecting higher levels of consumer spending.
